analysis.body:
# Grid Queue Snapshot: What AI Load Growth Means for Power Supply

Across five major US grid operators, approximately 1.3 million megawatts of generation and storage projects sit in interconnection queues as of mid-September 2026. Texas alone accounts for 438,086 MW through ERCOT, driven heavily by 150,347 MW of solar and 159,820 MW of storage—a combination that suggests grid operators are planning for concentrated, episodic demand rather than flat baseload. The Midcontinent (MISO) queue is the most fragmented by request count at 3,839 projects totaling 299,721 MW, while New York's smaller queue of 1,414 requests still represents 319,095 MW, underscoring regional variation in project scale. These queues reflect supply planning, not data center demand itself, but the rapid accumulation of storage and gas capacity typically precedes or accompanies large industrial load growth.

Commercial electricity sales across eight key states totaled 54,797 megawatt-hours in June 2026, with Texas accounting for 15,754 MWh at the lowest regional price of $8.66 per megawatt-hour. California consumed 10,025 MWh at the highest price of $27.33, while Virginia and Georgia each exceeded 5,500 MWh. Data centers are billed within the commercial class, so these figures serve as a proxy for overall commercial activity rather than a direct measurement of data center consumption. The price differentials—ranging from $8.66 in Texas to $27.33 in California—create clear incentives for compute-intensive operations to locate in lower-cost regions, a pattern the queue data partially reflects through Texas's outsized generation requests.

Gas-fired capacity in the queues totals roughly 184,544 MW across all five operators, with storage approaching 328,106 MW—a ratio that signals grid planners expect heavy cycling of fast-response resources to meet variable demand. Watch whether the storage-to-gas ratio continues shifting and which regions' solar-plus-storage projects advance fastest through their interconnection studies, as this will indicate where grid operators expect the next waves of concentrated consumption to land.
